kept.excerpt: On 23 August, Kazakhstan will vote for the Kurultai, a new 145-seat, single-chamber parliament. Its deputies will be elected entirely through national party lists, with a 5% threshold for representation and no constituency races or independent candidates. Adilet enters the race with the strongest organisational position after absorbing Amanat in June. Auyl has centred its campaign on rural Kazakhstan, food security, land reform and protections for agricultural workers.
kept.publisher: AnewZ — opinion by Nurbolat Nyshanbayev, Assistant Professor, Turan University
kept.relevance: Explains the seat-allocation framework, the dominant first-place contender and Auyl’s electoral positioning immediately before the cutoff.

kept.excerpt: Three national surveys place Adilet first and Auyl second ahead of the August 23 election. The Institute of Eurasian Integration interviewed 4,000 respondents face-to-face from July 16 to 26, reporting a margin of error no greater than 1.54%. It recorded Adilet at 65.1%, Auyl at 5.9%, Ak Zhol at 4.7%, Respublica at 4.6%, the NSDP at 4.2% and the People’s Party at 4.1%. An earlier DATAmetrics survey of 8,000 respondents recorded Auyl at 7.3%, ahead of Ak Zhol at 4.6% and Respublica at 3.4%.
kept.publisher: The Times of Central Asia — Andrei Matveev
kept.relevance: Provides multiple pre-cutoff polling measurements of Auyl’s lead over its closest competitors, including sample size and uncertainty for the latest survey discussed.

kept.excerpt: The Kazakhstan Institute of Public Development conducted a nationwide telephone survey of 1,200 respondents from July 8 to 20, 2026. Adilet received 64.8% support, Auyl 5.4%, Respublica 4.8% and Ak Zhol 4.7%. Auyl’s rural support was about 1.5 times its urban support. Another 10.9% of respondents remained undecided, while 2.2% intended to vote against all parties.
kept.relevance: Shows Auyl narrowly ahead of Respublica and Ak Zhol while identifying undecided voters and its rural support base as relevant uncertainties.

kept.excerpt: As of July 23, 2026, the lists of the seven political parties contesting seats in the Kurultai included a total of 545 candidates. The participating parties included Auyl. The election of deputies of the Kurultai was scheduled for August 23, 2026.
kept.publisher: Central Election Commission of the Republic of Kazakhstan
kept.relevance: Officially confirms the election schedule and the registered competitive field before the evidence cutoff.

kept.excerpt: The Central Election Commission registered Auyl’s party list for the Kurultai election scheduled for August 23, 2026. Auyl nominated 69 individuals, all of whom were found to meet constitutional and electoral-law requirements. The commission recalled that Auyl received 10.90% of the vote in the previous Mazhilis election, exempting it from the electoral deposit.
kept.publisher: Central Election Commission of the Republic of Kazakhstan
kept.relevance: Establishes Auyl’s eligibility to contest the election and supplies an official historical vote-share benchmark.

kept.excerpt: The last parliamentary elections were held early on March 19, 2023, with six of seven registered parties entering the Majilis. Amanat received 62 seats, Auyl eight, Ak Zhol and Respublika six each, the People’s Party five and the National Social-Democratic Party four; independent candidates won seven seats. Previous ODIHR reports noted that the political landscape was strongly dominated by the ruling party and that the distinction between the party and the executive branch was often blurred.
kept.publisher: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights
kept.relevance: Establishes Auyl’s second-place seat baseline in the preceding parliamentary election and provides institutional context for interpreting electoral competition.

search_notes: Frozen cutoff: 2026-08-11, inclusive. Included only sources with explicit publication dates on or before the cutoff; no election outcomes, exit polls, post-cutoff developments, prediction-market pages, betting odds or market prices are included. Excerpts are factual summaries of source text, not necessarily verbatim quotations. The Times of Central Asia page displays both August 4 and August 5, 2026; the later article-header date is used conservatively, and both precede the cutoff. The CEC’s July 23 publication date was corroborated in its official news and press-release indexes. Poll figures are reported respondent shares and have not been converted into valid-vote shares or seat forecasts; the surveys differ in methods and undecided shares and are not independent evidence when repeated by another publication.
